Thanks, Chair, distinguished delegates. Space exploration represents a major challenge to humanity in our quest to explore new frontiers, gain knowledge, and extend human presence deeper into space. Japan has been proud to participate in this challenging endeavor in close cooperation with our international partners. Chair, allow me to illustrate some of Japan's efforts in this regard. Japan is actively engaged in both domestic and international initiatives. In support of the Artemis program, Japan is committed to developing a crewed pressurized rover and implementing arrangement under the framework agreement between Japan and the United States. In parallel, Japan is advancing the lunar polar exploration mission, LUPEX, in collaboration with ISRO, NASA, and ESA. This mission aims to investigate the presence of water and assess the potential for resource utilization in the lunar polar region. Beyond the Moon, the Martian Moon Exploration, MMX mission, currently under development with NASA, CNES, ESA, and DLR to launch in autumn this year, will be the world's first collaborative scientific mission to collect samples from Phobos, one of the Martian moons. Also, BepiColombo, the ESA/JAXA joint mission, which was launched in 2018, will reach Mercury this winter, and the JAXA's orbiter, MMO, will be separated to begin scientific observation. In the area of planetary defense, Japan continues to actively contribute to addressing this as a shared challenge for all humankind, while fully considering the intent behind the United Nations designation of International Year of Asteroid Awareness and Planetary Defense. JAXA is contributing to international efforts by collaborating with ESA on the Hera mission, as well as conducting an asteroid observation this summer, during the asteroid flyby of JAXA's Hayabusa2 extended mission. Furthermore, JAXA and ESA have begun collaborating on the joint mission, Rabbit Apophis Mission for Space Safety, RAMSIS, which aims to explore the asteroid Apophis as it passes close to our planet on 13th April 2029. Together with our international partners, Japan is committed to taking part in this extraordinary journey by offering our technical expertise for the benefit of all of humanity. Chair, distinguished delegates. We live in an exciting time for humanity as we continue our exploration into the solar system and humans return to the lunar vicinity. Thanks to novel technology built upon centuries of innovation inspired by looking up at the stars, humanity is expanding its presence further than any human has gone before. The UK has a long history in space exploration. As a founding member of the European Space Agency, we pursue exploration through international collaboration and national investment. As a signatory to the Artemis Accords, we are also committed to promoting sustainable practices in exploration. We have a leading role in ESA's Rosalind Franklin mission to Mars with several UK-built instruments and the rover itself constructed by Airbus UK set to launch in 2028 and due to arrive at the red planet in 2030 to search for signs of life. The UK also plays a significant role in many other current or planned missions. For example, we are a key contributor to the Mars Trace Gas Orbiter, which currently acts as a vital communications relay, sending back over half of all the science data from the NASA rovers. The UK is leading the development of the engines and propulsion systems for Argonaut, Europe's first lunar lander, which will allow Europe to land up to 1.5 tons of cargo onto the lunar surface. We are leading the world in the development of the americium based solar space nuclear capabilities, specifically radioisotope power systems through ESA's Endure program. These power systems will support long duration missions and unlock exploration to environments in which a sustained presence is not currently possible. The UK also has a strong and diverse science community with advanced capabilities in understanding and mitigating the impacts of the space environment on human health, providing real world health innovations for people down here on Earth, alongside deep expertise in planetary science, supporting missions to the moon and Mars, attempting to answer fundamental philosophical questions like, are we alone in the universe? Our researchers play key roles in international programs, including collaboration on ESA's prospect lunar resource payload and scientific representation as one of only two international academics on the Artemis IV geology team. The UK has further invested in the ESA Moonlight program to deliver commercial lunar communications and navigation services, enabling reliable operations and supporting a sustainable, internationally accessible lunar economy. In addition to our work with ESA, the UK also collaborates across a number of bilateral exploration missions. International collaboration is a key tenet of the UK's approach to exploration and is becoming ever more important with humanity's renewed interest in the moon. With more actors pursuing lunar missions, it is increasingly important to share operational experience in this challenging environment. Insights from upcoming missions, including the UK's Lunar Pathfinder, should inform ATLAS principles to support safe and responsible exploration. However, beyond the ATLAS mandate, there is no clear forum for these issues to be discussed. There is therefore value in continuing a broader coordinated dialogue that engages diverse expertise and institutions while remaining mindful of UNISA's existing resources and priorities. Together, we can explore what one nation alone cannot, going further into the universe than ever before. Thank you, Chair.
